extracted.intended_audience: administrative law scholars, agency lawyers, and policymakers concerned with rulemaking and adjudication
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and apply procedural and substantive standards courts and the executive branch impose on agency rulemaking and adjudication, including administrative record rules, deference doctrines, and executive-order and statutory analytical requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: APA preamble requirement — 'concise general statement of basis and purpose'
rubrics_metrics.description: The Administrative Procedure Act requires a 'concise general statement of . . . basis and purpose' that enables courts to see what major issues of policy were ventilated by the informal proceedings and why the agency reacted as it did.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts do not expect agencies to discuss every item of fact or opinion in submissions, but they do expect preambles to disclose the major issues and the agency's rationale so judicial review is meaningful. Failure to address major issues can lead to remand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Automotive Parts precedent on preamble length and extra-record evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Automotive Parts declared that preambles can be as long as courts require to flesh out issues raised in litigation, effectively placing no practical limit on preamble length.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This precedent encourages agencies to draft expansive, highly detailed preambles; courts have treated use of extra-record evidence as potentially 'fatal error' (e.g., Seacoast Anti-Pollution League), so agencies often include extensive material in preambles rather than relying on post-litigation evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overton Park: contemporaneous rationales (no post-hoc rationalizations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts are to look at the contemporaneous rationales of agencies when reviewing their actions, rather than any 'post hoc' rationalizations conjured in litigation to support their positions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies must thoroughly document their rationales at the time a decision is made; courts have held affidavits alone insufficient to supply the agency's contemporaneous reasons (Overton Park).

rubrics_metrics.name: Overton Park: full administrative record review
rubrics_metrics.description: A court's review is to be based on the full administrative record that was before the agency at the time the decision was made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Review based on the administrative record limits agencies' ability to introduce new evidence in litigation and requires careful documentation and record-building during the agency's decision process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hard look review / reasoned decisionmaking
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts require agencies to take a 'hard look' at salient problems and to engage in genuine, reasoned decisionmaking; agencies fail when they have not really taken a hard look.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'hard look' standard demands a more complete record and a clearly articulated rationale to facilitate review for arbitrariness and caprice; agencies must focus on values served by decisions and avoid unconscious preferences or irrelevant prejudice (Greater Boston Television and subsequent cases).

rubrics_metrics.name: State Farm arbitrary-and-capricious grounds
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency action may be overturned if the agency (1) relied on factors Congress did not intend it to consider, (2) entirely failed to consider an important aspect of the problem, (3) offered an explanation running counter to the evidence before the agency, or (4) provided an explanation so implausible that it could not be ascribed to a difference in view or agency expertise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts will not supply missing reasons for the agency (Chenery II); failure to articulate consideration of aspects courts deem important can be dispositive. These grounds open opportunities for judicial reversal if the agency's rationale is deficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to respond to comments and address potentially significant criticisms in preambles
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies must consider and respond to substantive comments; failing to address even tangentially-related information in preambles can result in rules being overturned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulated parties learned to submit lengthy, detailed comments (often with consultants' reports) to attack proposed rules; if agencies fail to respond in preambles, courts may remand rules for insufficiency without allowing agencies to cure deficiencies after finalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive Order 12,866: cost–benefit and OIRA review for significant rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Executive Order 12,866 requires agencies (except independent agencies) to promulgate only regulations required by law or necessary to address compelling public needs and subjects many rulemakings to stringent cost–benefit analysis and White House (OIRA) approval.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Significant rules must have Regulatory Impact Analyses (RIAs) at the proposal stage, be submitted to OIRA for review and oversight, and receive OIRA approval before publication; the executive-order process can add months or years to rulemaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'significant rules' under EO 12,866
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'significant rule' is one that (1) may have an annual effect on the economy of $100 million or more or adversely affect other major interests, (2) creates serious inconsistency with other agency action, (3) materially alters budgetary impact of federal programs, or (4) raises novel legal or policy issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This definition determines which rules require RIAs and OIRA review; OIRA's designation and review authority substantially affects the regulatory timeline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory Impact Analysis (RIA) requirements and OIRA review timing
rubrics_metrics.description: At the proposal stage of significant rulemakings, agencies must complete RIAs assessing and, to the extent possible, quantifying anticipated costs and benefits, then submit proposed rules and RIAs to OIRA for review; OIRA has 90 days (with one 30-day extension or other extensions at agency request) to review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OIRA frequently exceeds the 90-day window and may control extension requests; delays are common and can be substantial (examples: more than 20% delayed >120 days; some delayed years), with significant public health and other consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory Flexibility Act (RFA) analyses for small entities
rubrics_metrics.description: The RFA requires agencies to analyze impacts on small businesses when publishing most rules, conducting two regulatory flexibility analyses—one at proposed rule stage and one for the final rule—estimating the number of small businesses affected and compliance requirements, and proposing/assessing alternatives to minimize significant economic impacts on small entities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Initial analyses must offer alternatives that accomplish statutory objectives while minimizing impact; final analyses must respond to comments and describe factual, policy, and legal reasons for selecting the adopted alternative. Courts can overturn rules for RFA noncompliance and may remand rules for supplemental RFA analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: SBREFA requirements: small entity compliance guides and review panels
rubrics_metrics.description: SBREFA requires agencies to issue small entity compliance guides accompanying final rules subject to the RFA and requires EPA, CFPB, and OSHA, when issuing proposed rules, to convene review panels that meet with representatives of small entities and issue reports with recommendations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Review panels include agency staff, OIRA, OMB, and SBA Office of Advocacy; in practice attendees often include trade associations that represent a range of firms, and the panels add procedural steps prior to finalizing rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Congressional Review Act (CRA) effects on rule durability and timing
rubrics_metrics.description: The CRA allows Congress to overturn any regulation via a simple majority resolution within sixty days of enactment and delays the effective date of 'major rules' for sixty days.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because CRA repeal resolutions are not filibusterable in the Senate, the CRA increases the risk that rules will be overturned compared with policies articulated in adjudications; OIRA has also used CRA considerations to require independent agencies to perform RIAs by designating rules as 'major.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Chevron v. NRDC — defer when statute ambiguous and agency interpretation permissible
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Chevron, when a statute is silent or ambiguous with respect to an issue, the court asks whether the agency's answer is based on a permissible construction of the statute and will defer to reasonable agency interpretations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chevron rests on the view that agencies possess technical expertise and that policymaking is properly within the executive branch's competency. However, Chevron's domain has been narrowed by later cases limiting deference when APA rigor is absent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skidmore and Mead factors for non-Chevron deference
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts may apply Skidmore-like deference (power to persuade) by looking to 'the thoroughness evident in [an agency's] consideration, the validity of its reasoning, its consistency with earlier and later pronouncements,' and other factors that give the agency's view persuasive force; Mead identified degree of care, consistency, formality, relative expertness, and persuasiveness as relevant in deciding deference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mead clarified that Chevron deference is appropriate only for interpretations with 'legal force' and where Congress likely intended to delegate interpretive authority; otherwise courts weigh the agency's persuasiveness under Skidmore.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations on Chevron: formality and APA 'rigors' requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The Court has declined to grant full Chevron deference to agency interpretations that were not the product of 'the rigors of the Administrative Procedure Act,' particularly those not made through formal adjudication or notice-and-comment rulemaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases such as Christensen, Reno v. Koray, and Mead indicate courts will be less likely to defer to informal or less formal agency interpretations, emphasizing the role of procedural formality and congressional delegation in determining the level of deference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjudication formality vs. procedural safeguards for Chevron legitimacy
rubrics_metrics.description: The APA's formal/informal adjudication dichotomy (formal = subject to hearing procedures; informal = not) is less important than the actual quality of procedural safeguards in determining whether an adjudication can produce interpretations worthy of Chevron deference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some 'informal' adjudications have more procedural protections than 'formal' ones under APA; therefore, evaluating procedures and safeguards (notice, evidentiary opportunities, reasoned findings) is critical in assessing whether adjudication-based policy can claim Chevron legitimacy.
